itinerary.summary: A north-to-south run from IAH that threads Houston's oldest neighborhoods, then swings through River Oaks money before landing in the city's Little India. Lunch works best on Hillcroft around 12:30, with Rice Village or the Heights as backups.

narration.title: George Bush Intercontinental Airport
narration.text: That's George Bush Intercontinental behind us, the main international airport for greater Houston. It opened back in 1969 as plain Houston Intercontinental, then was renamed in 1997 for George H. W. Bush, the forty-first president and a Houston resident. We're about twenty-three miles north of downtown here, and flights leave this field for five continents.

narration.title: Heights Christian Church
narration.text: Just off the road here, at 1703 Heights Boulevard, is Heights Christian Church. It was built in 1927. The congregation moved to a new location in 1967 but kept ownership of this building and used it for community events, and it went onto the National Register of Historic Places in 1983. A good first look at the older Heights.

narration.title: Houston Heights
narration.text: We're rolling into Houston Heights, a community in northwest-central Houston. Here's something locals will tell you. When somebody says the Heights, they usually mean a whole cluster of neighborhoods next door, places like Norhill and Woodland Heights. Houston Heights itself is narrower than that, and it has its own history, distinct from its neighbors. It was Houston's first planned suburb, and you can still read that plan in the street grid, in the Victorian bungalows sitting up on their porches, and in the walkable strip of shops and cafes along Nineteenth Street. Since you like historic neighborhoods, this is the one to slow down for. Park once and walk Nineteenth Street end to end, then notice how fast the bungalow porches take over the moment you step off the commercial block.

narration.title: Gerald D. Hines Waterwall Park
narration.text: Up ahead in the Uptown District is the Gerald D. Hines Waterwall Park, a multi story sculptural fountain facing the south side of Williams Tower. Fountain and tower both came from John Burgee Architects with Philip Johnson, built as an amenity for the office building. It stayed privately owned until 2008, when the Uptown district bought it to keep it around for good.

narration.title: Gulfton, Houston
narration.text: As we pass, this is Gulfton, a little over three square miles tucked between the Loop six ten and Beltway eight. In the 1960s and seventies it went up fast, block after block of apartment complexes built for young people arriving from the Northeast and the Midwest to work the oil boom. Those complexes still set the shape of the place.

narration.title: Mahatma Gandhi District
narration.text: Welcome to the Mahatma Gandhi District, named for Mahatma Gandhi himself. It's an ethnic enclave made up mostly of Indian and Pakistani restaurants and shops, with a large South Asian population around it. Almost nobody uses the official name, though. Locals say Harwin, after Harwin Drive, the thoroughfare that carries most of the district. Or they say Hillcroft, after Hillcroft Avenue, which meets Interstate sixty-nine and is the main entrance for people coming up from Sugar Land and Missouri City. Hillcroft also holds a lot of the district's most popular South Asian businesses. You came to Houston partly for this, so give it the full hour. Walk one strip center end to end before you commit to anything, because the sweet houses and sari shops hide behind very plain storefronts.

narration.title: Arena Place
narration.text: Coming up in Sharpstown is Arena Place, two nineteen story office towers plus the Arena Theatre. The theater is the fun part. It's round, it seats about 2,850 people, and because of that circular shape no seat in the house is more than sixty-five feet from the stage. Hard to buy a bad ticket in a room like that.

narration.title: BAPS Shri Swaminarayan Mandir, Houston
narration.text: We're pulling up to the BAPS Shri Swaminarayan Mandir, a Hindu temple built by the BAPS Swaminarayan Sanstha. Its address is a small puzzle. The mandir stands in unincorporated Fort Bend County, inside the extraterritorial jurisdiction of Stafford, and its mail goes to a Stafford address, so it sits in the county and in the city's orbit at the same time. What people really come for is the stone. It is hand carved, Italian marble and Turkish limestone, and it is the single most striking Indian landmark in this whole region. Take a minute for your eyes to adjust once you step inside, then pick one pillar and follow its carving from the base all the way to the top.

narration.title: Southwest Inn fire
narration.text: Somewhere along this stretch of southwest Houston stood the Southwest Inn. On the thirty-first of May, 2013, a fire in an Indian restaurant there spread into the hotel next door and went to five alarms. Four firefighters were killed and thirteen more injured, the worst casualty loss the Houston Fire Department has ever taken. Captain Bill Dowling, who lost both legs that day, died of complications in 2017.

narration.title: Galleria Office Towers
narration.text: We're into the Uptown district now, and those big slabs of glass are the Galleria Office Towers, standing right on the Galleria site. Galleria Tower One runs twenty-five floors at 2700 Post Oak Boulevard, and Tower Two twenty-one floors at 5051 Westheimer Road. That's the address book of affluent Houston in a couple of buildings, and your hotel sits right in the thick of it.
